title: The Balanced Trap

scenario.situation: A fraud-detection model trained on a 50/50 rebalanced dataset is flagging roughly 30% of production transactions as fraudulent. The true fraud rate in production is about 2%.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The team assumes the model is basically sound and the fix is simple: nudge the classification threshold upward until the flag rate looks reasonable.
scenario.question: Why is the model over-predicting positives in production, and what is the right fix?

decisions.prompt: Your team wants to ship a threshold fix by end of week. How do you frame your investigation before touching anything?

options.label: Grid-search the threshold
options.detail: Try thresholds from 0.3 to 0.9 and pick the one that brings the flag rate closest to 2%.
options.consequence: You find a threshold that suppresses the flag rate — but the underlying probabilities are still inflated and miscalibrated. You've hidden the symptom without treating the cause; precision and recall will drift as the production distribution shifts.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored on the team's hypothesis and masked the miscalibration rather than diagnosing it.

options.label: Calibration diagnostic
options.detail: Check whether the model's predicted probabilities match observed fraud rates across score bins — a reliability diagram / calibration curve on held-out production data.
options.consequence: The calibration plot reveals a systematic upward shift: bins the model scores at 0.5 have an actual fraud rate near 0.02. This is a uniform inflation pattern, not random noise — a strong signal that the prior was changed at training time and never corrected.

options.label: Feature drift audit
options.detail: Compare training feature distributions to production feature distributions to look for covariate shift.
options.consequence: Feature distributions look similar — no obvious covariate shift. You've ruled out one cause but spent time on the wrong thread; the problem was never in the features.
options.divergenceCost: Chased covariate shift when the mismatch was in the label prior, not the features.

options.label: Collect more labeled production data and retrain
options.detail: Label a fresh production sample and retrain without rebalancing.
options.consequence: Retraining will eventually help, but it takes weeks and doesn't explain *why* the current model is miscalibrated. You've bypassed diagnosis entirely and will repeat the mistake on the next model.
options.divergenceCost: Jumped to retraining before understanding the mechanism — the same mistake will recur.

decisions.prompt: You pull model scores for 10,000 production transactions alongside their true labels. Which metric do you use to confirm what's wrong?

artifact.title: Raw positive predictions by score bucket — production sample
artifact.caption: Most predictions pile up in the 0.4–0.8 range. Does this mean fraud is really that common, or is something else going on?

options.label: Flag rate (share of transactions scored above 0.5)
options.detail: Count what fraction of production transactions the model calls positive.
options.consequence: The flag rate is 34% — obviously too high. But this only confirms the problem exists; it says nothing about whether the scores themselves are valid probabilities or systematically inflated. Threshold-tuning looks like the obvious next step.
options.divergenceCost: Measured the symptom, not the mechanism — leaves the root cause invisible.

options.label: Observed fraud rate vs. mean predicted probability per score bin (calibration curve)
options.detail: For each score decile, compute actual fraud rate among those transactions and plot it against the model's mean predicted score.
options.consequence: The calibration curve shows every bin is inflated by roughly the same multiplicative factor: transactions scored 0.50 have a true fraud rate of only 0.019. The inflation ratio (~25×) matches almost exactly what prior-adjustment theory predicts when a 2% base rate is rebalanced to 50%. The fix is algebraic, not empirical.

artifact.title: Observed fraud rate vs. model score bin — production sample
artifact.caption: Observed fraud rates (%) per bin. A model predicting 50% probability sees only ~2% actual fraud — a ~25× inflation consistent with a prior shift from 2% to 50% at training time.

decisions.prompt: The calibration curve shows uniform score inflation matching the rebalancing ratio. What do you tell the team?

options.label: "Resampling caused this — apply the prior-adjustment formula and ship it."
options.detail: State the cause with confidence and push the algebraic correction directly to production.
options.consequence: The formula is almost certainly right, but shipping a probability correction to a live fraud system without a shadow-mode validation is a real operational risk. If any other factor is also inflating scores, the correction will be wrong in an invisible way.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed certainty and skipped the validation step before a production change.

options.label: "The calibration pattern matches prior-shift theory almost exactly — resampling is the most likely cause. Let's apply the prior-adjustment correction in shadow mode and validate on a held-out week before promoting it."
options.detail: Name the mechanism, recommend the algebraic fix, and require a shadow-mode holdout before going live.
options.consequence: You've given the team a precise, theoretically grounded explanation that reframes the 'threshold nudge' framing entirely, while protecting production with a validation gate. Shadow results confirm the correction brings calibration error near zero — and the team now understands why rebalancing requires a corresponding serving-time correction.

insight: When you oversample to balance classes, you implicitly change the prior the model learns — from the true 2% base rate to 50%. Served in production without correction, every predicted probability is inflated by a factor of roughly (p_train / p_true) × ((1 − p_true) / (1 − p_train)), making the model look wildly over-confident. A threshold adjustment hides this but does not fix it; the correct remedy is prior adjustment (or Platt/isotonic calibration) applied at serving time. The lesson: resampling is a training convenience, not a free lunch — the serving environment still has the original prior, and your model must be corrected to match it.
